title: Redgrave v. Boston Symphony Orchestra, Inc. — En Banc Appeal
lead: The Boston Symphony Orchestra canceled Vanessa Redgrave’s engagement after political protests; the en banc court allowed narrowly proved lost-work damages but upheld rejection of her separate state civil-rights claim.

actors.name: Vanessa Redgrave
actors.role: Actor engaged to narrate Oedipus Rex and plaintiff in contract and civil-rights claims

actors.name: Boston Symphony Orchestra (BSO)
actors.role: Orchestra canceling the engagement and performances

actors.name: Redgrave’s company
actors.role: Coplaintiff on the contract claim only

actors.name: Theodore Mann
actors.role: Producer whose testimony supported one lost theatrical opportunity

proceedings: Jury found breach and consequential loss; district court awarded stipulated fee but set aside $100,000 consequential award and rejected civil-rights liability; after state certification and a withdrawn panel decision, en banc court affirmed civil-rights judgment and remanded contract judgment for $12,000 less expenses in supported consequential damages.
limits: Five judges agreed on contract analysis; three upheld the civil-rights result and two dissented. The court left the federal constitutional defense to the civil-rights claim undecided. It authorized no retrial to prove the discarded balance of consequential damages.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Political protests preceded cancellation of the contracted concerts
sections.cue: Introduce the engagement and the orchestra’s asserted reasons.
paragraphs: In March 1982, the Boston Symphony Orchestra (BSO) engaged Vanessa Redgrave to narrate Oedipus Rex concerts in Boston and New York. Subscribers and others protested her support for the Palestine Liberation Organization and her views concerning Israel. Around April 1, BSO canceled both her engagement and the performances. It asserted audience and performer safety, disruption, and artistic-integrity concerns, rather than a purpose to punish her speech.

After a sixteen-day trial, a jury found breach and foreseeable career harm. The district court awarded the stipulated $27,500 net performance fee. It thought evidence sufficient for the jury’s additional $100,000 consequential award but set that award aside using expression protections drawn from defamation law. Acting advisorially on the Massachusetts Civil Rights Act claim, the jury found that BSO’s own political disagreement did not motivate cancellation. The court also rejected liability merely for yielding to outsiders.

Redgrave appealed damages and civil rights; BSO cross-appealed the sufficiency of consequential proof. Her company joined only the contract claim. The First Circuit certified state-law questions to Massachusetts’s Supreme Judicial Court, received answers, and issued a divided panel decision. It withdrew that opinion and dissent for en banc reconsideration of civil rights, while incorporating and reaffirming the panel’s contract analysis in this later decision.

sections.title: Specific lost engagements could support contract damages
sections.cue: Distinguish identifiable income from a price placed on general reputation.
paragraphs: Judge Coffin’s en banc opinion rejected a categorical prohibition on the contract damages Redgrave sought. Cases denying reputational damages usually turned on remoteness, foreseeability, and speculative valuation. Her theory instead identified film or theater engagements she would have received but for the breach. Such financial opportunities could meet Massachusetts requirements of natural consequence, reasonable foreseeability, and rational calculation on firm evidence. The instructions properly required but-for causation, natural and probable consequences, and contemplation when contracting.

The district court’s added expression hurdle did not apply here. It had reasoned that learning of cancellation necessarily communicated a message and therefore required a materially false factual statement made knowingly or recklessly. But BSO did not intend symbolic speech or a message about Redgrave. Its press release avoided such implications and did not name her, and the jury rejected the particular implied opinion presented to it.

Information about an act differed from intentional expression through the act. Another employer might infer something from cancellation even when BSO intended no message. Ordinary demanding contract-damage rules therefore governed, without the defamation-derived requirement. The court reserved whether an intentionally expressive cancellation might ever receive First Amendment protection.

sections.title: The film and most theater evidence did not establish causal losses
sections.cue: Explain why favorable verdict review still rejected most of the amount.
paragraphs: The court viewed proof favorably to Redgrave and respected reasonable inferences, while considering uncontradicted opposing evidence. Her claimed fourteen-month collapse in secure film opportunities did not fit three accepted offers totaling $850,000 had production occurred. Annie’s Coming Out offered $250,000; expecting it to proceed, she declined apparently secure work including Yellowbeard and Who Will Love My Children? No Alternatives offered $350,000 and eventually produced a $25,000 forfeiture payment. Track 39 offered $250,000. All failed financially, without sufficient proof linking their production failures to BSO.

Earlier-work comparisons often identified actual performances rather than the number or security of offers. Even a decline in quality needed to be separated from producers’ preexisting political concerns; Redgrave acknowledged lost work from controversy before BSO, and changing agents offered another explanation. No film producer directly attributed a lost opportunity to the cancellation.

Most American theater proof likewise lacked producer explanations or ascertainable pay. Three anticipated productions or opportunities failed to materialize, some never reaching Broadway. Redgrave had received no Broadway offers in 1981 and historically accepted only one of many American theater offers. That weakened inferences both of a sudden decline and of work she necessarily would have accepted.

sections.title: One producer tied a calculable engagement to BSO’s example
sections.cue: State the precise additional recovery the evidence permitted.
paragraphs: Theodore Mann’s testimony about Heartbreak House differed. He said he decided against hiring Redgrave partly because a premier institution with similar financial support had canceled. One inference was independent fear of controversy; another was that BSO’s example influenced his decision. The latter reasonably supported the jury’s causation finding and had to be respected on review.

Mann identified a contemplated $12,000 fee. That opportunity supported consequential damages reduced by expenses Redgrave herself would have incurred performing it. The court did not award $12,000 for generalized reputational injury or authorize the gross fee without expense adjustment.

sections.title: The state court rejected simple acquiescence as a civil-rights defense
sections.cue: Explain why the federal majority nevertheless upheld that judgment on another ground.
paragraphs: The Massachusetts Civil Rights Act reached private interference with secured rights through threats, intimidation, or coercion. In response to certification, the state court explained that yielding to third-party pressure could create liability without a personal desire to interfere. Fear of economic loss, business disruption, or physical harm did not provide abstract justification, although explicit imminent physical danger was reserved because absent from the certified premise. Those answers defeated the district court’s acquiescence rationale.

The en banc majority nevertheless read additional observations in the state plurality, concurrence, and dissent as indicating that Massachusetts law would deny liability in this artistic setting. It identified rather than collapsed those positions: the concurrence relied on a state constitutional right to select artistic works, while the dissent construed the statute more narrowly and questioned whether cancellation threatened future BSO action. Applying constitutional avoidance, the federal majority predicted a state statutory or constitutional bar.

Its discussion addressed tension between the performer’s speech protection and the orchestra’s control of artistic expression, including a right not to perform. But the civil-rights result rested on its understanding of state law. It expressly declined to decide the existence or content of a federal First Amendment defense, a different question from the rejected expression hurdle to ordinary contract damages.

sections.title: Bownes and Selya disputed the state-law prediction and broad artistic immunity
sections.cue: Attribute the dissent and give the divided mandate.
paragraphs: Judges Bownes and Selya fully agreed with contract analysis but dissented on civil rights. Bownes objected to constructing a state-law bar from incompatible minority positions and remarks on questions the state plurality reserved. Certification answered legal questions, he argued; it did not permit prediction of an aggregate result assembled from those votes. His discussion of Michigan v. Long, concerning state and federal grounds, challenged the majority’s characterization and urged confronting the unresolved constitutional issues.

On those issues, the dissent recognized artistic freedom but rejected an expansive artistic-integrity defense. Applying the statute to an orchestra yielding to hostile outside pressure could advance a compelling interest in political expression without dictating content. Drawing on antidiscrimination decisions and distinguishing actual cancellation from political symbolic speech, the dissent warned of a heckler’s veto and immunity for discrimination merely labeled artistic judgment. It acknowledged that other settings, such as newspaper editorial control, might differ.

On August 31, 1988, the five-judge court unanimously adopted the contract ruling, with Coffin, Breyer, and Torruella forming the civil-rights majority against Bownes and Selya. It affirmed judgment for BSO on civil rights, vacated the contract judgment, and remanded for the supported consequential award of $12,000 less expenses, retaining the stipulated $27,500 performance-fee recovery. No appellate costs were awarded, and no new trial was ordered to prove the discarded balance of $100,000.
